Acids and Bases.intro: Acids and bases are fundamental in chemistry. The pH scale measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is.

sections.title: The pH Scale
points: pH 0-6 = acidic (H⁺ ions)
pH 7 = neutral
pH 8-14 = alkaline (OH⁻ ions)
Strong acids/alkalis fully ionise; weak acids/alkalis partially ionise
Universal indicator or pH meter to measure pH

sections.title: Reactions of Acids
points: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen
Acid + metal oxide → salt + water
Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water (neutralisation)
Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide

keyTerms.def: A substance that produces H⁺ ions in solution; pH below 7
A soluble base that produces OH⁻ ions; pH above 7
Reaction between an acid and a base to form salt and water
An ionic compound formed when an acid reacts with a base

examTips: Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water. Remember this general equation.
The name of the salt depends on the acid: HCl → chloride, H₂SO₄ → sulphate, HNO₃ → nitrate.
commonMistakes: Confusing acid + carbonate (also makes CO₂) with acid + metal oxide (no CO₂).

Salts.intro: Salts are ionic compounds formed from neutralisation reactions. Making pure dry salt requires specific practical techniques.

sections.title: Making Salts
points: Soluble salts made by reacting acid with excess solid base/carbonate/metal
Filter off excess solid
Evaporate solution to crystallise salt
Insoluble salts made by precipitation — mixing two solutions

sections.title: Naming Salts
points: Named from the acid and the base
HCl → chloride; H₂SO₄ → sulphate; HNO₃ → nitrate
NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O (sodium chloride)

keyTerms.def: The process of forming crystals from a saturated solution
Formation of an insoluble solid from two solutions

examTips: For making soluble salts: use EXCESS base to ensure all acid reacts, then filter off excess base.
Precipitation: mix solutions containing the required ions.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to add excess base to neutralise all the acid.

Reactivity Series.intro: The reactivity series ranks metals from most to least reactive. It can be used to predict displacement reactions and the stability of metal compounds.

sections.title: The Reactivity Series
points: Potassium > Sodium > Calcium > Magnesium > Aluminium > Zinc > Iron > Copper > Silver > Gold
More reactive metals: react vigorously with water/acid; form stable oxides
Less reactive metals: react slowly or not at all; found native (uncombined) in Earth

sections.title: Displacement Reactions
points: More reactive metal displaces less reactive from compound
Example: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu (zinc displaces copper)
Used to extract metals: aluminium displaces iron in thermite reaction

keyTerms.def: A list of metals in order of decreasing reactivity
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from a compound

examTips: Use MASH CuSG as a mnemonic: Mg Al Zn Fe Cu (most to least reactive of common metals).
Only a MORE reactive metal can displace a LESS reactive one.
commonMistakes: Saying a less reactive metal displaces a more reactive one — this cannot happen.

Redox.intro: Redox reactions involve the simultaneous transfer of electrons. Oxidation and reduction always occur together.

callout.label: Memory Aid
callout.text: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons)

sections.title: Oxidation States
points: Oxidation: loss of electrons; increase in oxidation number
Reduction: gain of electrons; decrease in oxidation number
Reducing agent: gives electrons (gets oxidised)
Oxidising agent: takes electrons (gets reduced)

keyTerms.def: Loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen)
Gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen)
Reaction involving simultaneous oxidation and reduction
Oxidation Is Loss; Reduction Is Gain — memory aid for electron transfer

examTips: OIL RIG — learn this! Oxidation and reduction always happen together.
Reducing agent gets OXIDISED; oxidising agent gets REDUCED.
commonMistakes: Confusing which species is oxidised and which is reduced.

Electrolysis.intro: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to break down ionic compounds. It is used to extract reactive metals and purify copper.

sections.title: How Electrolysis Works
points: Ionic compound must be MOLTEN or DISSOLVED in water
Positive ions (cations) move to negative electrode (cathode) — reduced
Negative ions (anions) move to positive electrode (anode) — oxidised
At cathode: metal deposited OR hydrogen gas produced
At anode: oxygen produced (from solution) OR halogen gas

sections.title: Products from Electrolysis
points: Molten ionic compound: metal at cathode, non-metal at anode
Sodium chloride solution (brine): hydrogen at cathode, chlorine at anode, sodium hydroxide remains
Copper sulphate solution: copper at cathode, oxygen at anode

keyTerms.def: Decomposition of an ionic compound using electricity
Negative electrode — where reduction occurs (positive ions discharged)
Positive electrode — where oxidation occurs (negative ions discharged)
The molten or dissolved ionic compound that is electrolysed

examTips: Cathode = negative = metals/hydrogen produced. Anode = positive = non-metals/oxygen produced.
If electrolysing a solution: hydrogen may form at cathode instead of metal if metal is more reactive than hydrogen.
commonMistakes: Confusing anode (positive, oxidation) and cathode (negative, reduction).
